title: karma: a service capstone — a year designed and reviewed
hook: a calendar with every square filled, and a verse about food, sleep and the pace of work
carry: karma: a service capstone — a year designed and reviewed
tomorrow: a teacher's send-off says give with fear. why fear?

segments.voice: Yesterday, karma with the world in view: lokasangraha, small work that helps hold the world together. Today, how fast a year of it can run.

The calendar is taped to the bedroom wall, and it's beautiful. Green squares for the food pantry, every Saturday. Blue for tutoring, every weeknight. Orange for early errands for the neighbor down the hall. Not one white square left. Its maker steps back, proud, and then a small cold thought arrives. What happens on the week of exams? The week of the flu? Krishna has an answer for that wall, and he gives it in the middle of a lesson on meditation, of all places.
screen: `EVERY SQUARE FILLED.` → `THE WEEK OF THE FLU?` → `KRISHNA HAS AN ANSWER.`

segments.voice: In chapter six of the Bhagavad Gita, Krishna is teaching Arjuna how to sit and steady the mind. Then he turns practical. Yoga, he says, isn't for the one who eats too much, or for the one who doesn't eat at all. It isn't for the one who sleeps too much, or the one who's always awake. Then the key line, in paraphrase: for the one who is measured in eating and resting, measured in effort at work, measured in sleep and waking, yoga becomes the end of sorrow. The Sanskrit for measured is yukta: fitted, joined, in proportion. Look at what sits in the middle of that list. Effort in actions. The Gita puts the pace of work right beside food and sleep, as one balance. That's the second design rule for a year of service: size it so it lasts. The beautiful wall breaks on its first tired week, and a plan that drains someone by spring helps nobody in the fall. So the designer works like a good coach: an amount that can be kept on a bad week, and rest that's planned, not stolen. This isn't a lower bar. The measured person isn't doing less of what matters. They're doing it at a pace the body and the household can carry, so it's still being done when the year runs out.
screen: `NOT TOO MUCH, NOT TOO LITTLE.` · `YUKTA: MEASURED, IN PROPORTION.` · `WORK SITS BESIDE FOOD AND SLEEP.` · then, large: `SIZE IT SO IT LASTS.`

segments.voice: On paper or in a note, write one kind thing you already do that's small enough to keep up on your most tired week. Under it, write when you'll rest from it. Then breathe at an easy pace, not long, not short, with the page in front of you.
Karma: action, kept in measure like food and sleep, so a year of service is still going at its end.
Keep this: karma, a year designed and reviewed, and sized to last. Day three of the capstone, done.

howItsDone: Hindu teachers who draw on Gita 6.16–17 counsel balance in food, sleep and work, so that practice and service can be steady over a lifetime rather than intense for a season.
